|Failure mode|What happens in practice|Why it costs a provider|
|**Repeated prefill**|The same repo facts, traces, and file summaries are reprocessed every related turn.|More compute before the first output token; higher latency on long prompts.|
|**KV-cache growth**|Every unnecessary input token contributes attention state.|Higher memory pressure → lower concurrency, harder scheduling.|
|**Cache misses**|Stable repo facts are mixed with task text, timestamps, logs, and tool output.|Prompt caching and prefix reuse stop working.|
|**Stale context**|Old decisions and obsolete docs get retrieved because they look relevant.|Wrong patches, repeat loops, lower trust in agent output.|
|**Unmanaged memory**|Memory grows with no proof, lifecycle, or contradiction handling.|Persistent memory becomes a reliability and security risk.|

|**MemoryIR**|A formal IR for repo facts, decisions, traces, tests — each with source anchor, trust, freshness, sensitivity, token cost, and cache role.|Every pack is an explainable compiled artifact, not a loose bundle of text.|

|**Stable prefix + fresh suffix**|Durable repo knowledge is separated from volatile task state, logs, and errors. The stable prefix excludes task text and is `blake3`-hashed.|Same repo state → same prefix across tasks → real prompt-cache reuse.|
|**Negative memory**|Stale docs, wrong fixes, generated files, misleading traces, and superseded decisions are remembered as *exclusions*.|The model gets less harmful context, not just more context.|
|**Freshness proofs**|Memories are tied to source files, hashes, commits, tests, or human confirmation.|Old or unsupported memories are rejected before they enter the prompt.|
|**KV-aware optimizer**|Context is scored by `utility / cost`, where cost includes tokens and volatility — not relevance alone.|Small high-signal facts beat large weakly-useful files.|
|**Rehydratable handles**|Packs can ship compact facts plus `mem://file/...#L10-L50` handles.|Exact code is loaded only when needed; tiny upfront token load.|
|**Ledger + lockfile**|Every pack records included/excluded memory, proof state, cache regions, and hashes.|Agent context becomes reproducible and auditable.|

- `text` links to the `pages` document whose slug is `install`. You can only name documents you can read; anything else gets the same 422 as a slug that doesn't exist. One write names at most 1,000 documents this way.
- `<u>…</u>` is underline and ` ` (or ` `, ` `) is a hard break. That's all the HTML there is.

Markdown that doesn't fit is refused with a 422 and the line it's on, never half-converted: `line 3: raw HTML isn't allowed; the only tags are <u>…</u> and `, or ``line 3: unknown directive `:::aside` ``. A value can be up to 1 MiB, a numbered list starts at 1,000,000 at most, a NUL character is refused anywhere, and so is a directive straight after a task box (`- [ ] ::cta{…}`). Some things have no Markdown at all: subscript and superscript come out as plain text, and cell spans and `newTab` are dropped.
- A table cell holding several blocks, or one block that isn't a paragraph, becomes one paragraph, with ` ` between the blocks.

A link to a document goes to its collection's `url`, here `/{slug}`; without one, it's the link text alone. Block fields become `data-*` attributes (`ctaLabel` is `data-cta-label`), and anything that isn't a plain value is written as JSON. A relationship node is a ` ` around the linked document's first text field. Text is escaped, every `href` is checked again on the way out, and `newTab` links get `target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer"`. As `text`, you get the words alone, the rich text inside block nodes included.

- **Many writers stop waiting on each other.** When goroutines write at the same time, the driver runs their autocommit `INSERT`, `UPDATE` and `DELETE` statements as one transaction and commits once. Each call still gets its own error, `LastInsertId` and `RowsAffected`, and returns only after the commit, so nothing is less durable. When one statement fails so badly that SQLite rolls back the whole transaction (an IO error, `ON CONFLICT ROLLBACK`, a context that ends while it runs), the statements merged before it fail with `ABORT_ROLLBACK`, and none runs twice. Al compilarse directamente a código máquina nativo, Félix no requiere una máquina virtual V8 ni un intérprete de Python en memoria constante. Con un consumo en reposo inferior a 25 MB de RAM, coexiste pacíficamente en servidores que ya ejecutan bases de datos, aplicaciones web y servicios contenerizados sin disputar recursos.

Mientras otras herramientas delegan la edición y prueba de código en llamadas externas pesadas o editores interactivos de terminal, Félix incorpora internamente el motor de análisis sintáctico AST (`repomap` que resume repositorios en < 1.500 tokens), el motor de parcheo difuso tolerante a discrepancias de sangría y el sandbox atómico en ramas efímeras de Git.

A diferencia de agentes que abortan abruptamente con errores de timeout cuando una herramienta previa demora o cuando la API principal agota cuota, Félix implementa Fast-Failover a los 20 segundos con desacoplamiento de contexto (`context.WithoutCancel`) y 35 segundos garantizados para el proveedor de respaldo, respaldado por degradación elegante (`summarizeExecutedTools`) para rescatar los resultados del turno.

Félix está diseñado para ser administrado desde el teléfono celular o la terminal a través de WhatsApp y Telegram, permitiendo dar órdenes en lenguaje natural o recibir reportes técnicos detallados estés donde estés, con autenticación RBAC y confidencialidad de usuarios.

The same operations are exposed as **94 MCP tools** (`ragraf_*`) — for attachment to an agent as a server — and through the CLI. One group of tools is the live database layer: `ragraf_db_schema`, `ragraf_db_table`, `ragraf_db_relations`, `ragraf_db_sample`, `ragraf_db_drift`, `ragraf_db_cross`. One operation of the closed tier (enterprise edition) compares the declared design with the computed graph by FQN — `contract_drift` (modules, dependencies, contracts; every code-side divergence carries `file:line`) — and is declared as the tool `ragraf_contract_drift` (capability `contract-drift`). Two operations of the closed tier (enterprise edition) are declared as tools: `ragraf_license_offline` (offline licence: request, issue, acceptance, transfer) and `ragraf_attest_bundle` (delivery attestation: a signed evidence bundle and its verification). The quality loop (pro edition) is `ragraf_quality_suite` (an index check suite plus a run record), `ragraf_quality_diff` (divergences between two runs) and `ragraf_quality_prune` (thinning the run journal: a dry run by default, deletion only with confirmation and after a copy of the journal). Provenance (pro) adds two tools — `ragraf_doc_asof` (the edition in force on a date, with its validity interval and version id) and `ragraf_dependents` (what rested on a fact: the transitive walk, `outside_cap`, and the split between recomputing a derivation and a human decision). Three operations of the shared index (also pro) are outside the MCP set: they manage publication and the network channel rather than index reads, and run as `python -m ragraf.shared_index` (see `docs/03_implementation/SHARED-INDEX.md`). The secret broker (pro) is represented by two tools — `ragraf_broker_issue` (lease: term, custodian, reason, one-time redemption) and `ragraf_broker_rotate` (plan state, scheduling, rotation with lease revocation); lease state lives in `catalog/broker.json`, and the storage schema does not change.
